screens.title: Serverless Microservices with Lambda & API Gateway
screens.narratorSegment: Serverless microservices pair AWS Lambda with Amazon A P I Gateway to let you concentrate on business logic instead of servers. In this lesson you will learn the core roles each service plays, common integration patterns, and the operational levers you can use to tune performance and cost. We will walk through a concrete user-registration flow to illustrate asynchronous events, security via authorizers, and how to limit latency with provisioned concurrency. You will also see how integrations with DynamoDB, SQS and SNS enable resilient, decoupled microservices that scale automatically. A practical SAM deployment snippet and a short hands-on activity will show how to bootstrap a 'Hello World' A P I and validate it with curl. Finally, you will learn common mistakes to avoid — such as tight coupling between functions or underestimating cold start impact — and the safety principle of least privilege for IAM roles. By the end of this module you will be able to design a serverless microservice, choose the right A P I Gateway type, tune Lambda performance, secure endpoints, and reason about cost trade-offs. Consider how these ideas map to a user-facing A P I you manage and which knobs you would change first for latency or cost.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next screens we will achieve five practical objectives that equip you to design, optimize, secure, and operate serverless microservices. First, you will learn to design and implement serverless microservices using Lambda and A P I Gateway, with clear patterns for synchronous APIs and asynchronous event wiring. Second, you will optimize Lambda performance by understanding cold starts, tuning memory and C P U trade-offs, and managing concurrency so functions remain responsive. Third, you will secure serverless APIs using A P I Gateway authorizers — exploring Lambda authorizers, IAM authorizers, and Cognito user pools — and apply the principle of least privilege to execution roles. Fourth, you will integrate serverless microservices with other AWS services such as DynamoDB, SQS, SNS, and Step Functions to build durable, decoupled workflows. Finally, you will learn how to analyze cost drivers in serverless designs, right-size resources, and use features like provisioned concurrency judiciously. Each objective pairs a concept with a small practice or mental model so you can both reason about designs and apply them in real deployments. As you proceed, notice trade-offs between latency, cost, and operational complexity, and keep an eye on common mistakes such as tight coupling and missing IAM restrictions.

screens.title: AWS Lambda Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service that runs code in response to events. At its core, Lambda is event-driven and stateless: functions are invoked when triggers occur, execute business logic, and then return results or emit events. This stateless model is a strength for microservices because each function can be independently deployed and scaled without managing servers. A concrete example is a registration handler that validates input, writes to DynamoDB, and publishes an SNS event. In practice, treat Lambda as ephemeral compute: any persistent state must live in external services such as DynamoDB or S3. A common misconception is to assume in-memory state persists across invocations; while container reuse may appear to hold data, it is not guaranteed and should not be relied upon. Another important feature is pay-per-execution billing billed in 1 millisecond increments, which encourages small, focused functions. For performance, remember that memory allocation controls C P U allocation proportionally, so increasing memory can reduce execution time. Finally, when designing microservices, prefer clear single-responsibility functions and avoid tight coupling; where coordination is needed, use event mechanisms like SNS or Step Functions. Reflect on a service you maintain: what state must be externalized, and which events would you publish for decoupled processing?

Misconception

Pro tip

Visual: Function lifecycle
Event arrives

Auto-scaling per concurrent requests

screens.title: Amazon API Gateway — Types & Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon A P I Gateway is the managed front door for your serverless APIs. It comes in three main flavors: REST APIs, HTTP APIs, and WebSocket APIs. REST APIs provide the fullest feature set including stages, models, and integrations; they are useful when you need advanced A P I management features. HTTP APIs are a newer alternative offering lower latency and lower cost for common RESTful patterns; they are a good fit when you want simple routing and performance. WebSocket APIs enable bidirectional, low-latency communication for real-time applications. Choosing the right type matters: for a low-latency microservice that only needs simple request/response behavior, HTTP APIs often reduce cost and improve performance. For complex versioning, request/response transformations, or advanced monitoring you might prefer REST APIs. Authorizers are another dimension: A P I Gateway supports Lambda authorizers for custom logic, IAM authorizers to use AWS credentials, and Amazon Cognito User Pools for managed user directories. A common mistake is defaulting to the full REST A P I without checking if an HTTP A P I covers your requirements — this can increase cost and latency unnecessarily. Consider the chat, IoT, or simple CRUD A P I you maintain. Which Gateway type best balances your need for features versus latency and cost?

screens.title: Cold Starts & Provisioned Concurrency
screens.narratorSegment: A cold start occurs when Lambda must initialize a new execution environment before running your code. This includes setting up the runtime, pulling the code, and running any initialization logic. Cold starts are more visible for languages with heavier runtimes or large deployment packages, and for functions placed in a VPC where ENI provisioning can add latency. To mitigate cold starts, the primary tool is provisioned concurrency, which pre-initializes a defined number of execution environments so those invocations avoid cold initialization. Provisioned concurrency is ideal for latency-sensitive functions, but it increases cost because you pay for the pre-initialized environments whether they are used or not. Additional techniques include minimizing deployment package size, lazy-loading heavy dependencies, and reducing initialization work in the handler. Another approach is to use warmers or scheduled invocations to keep environments alive, but these are less reliable than provisioned concurrency and can add cost. A common misconception is to believe reserved concurrency eliminates cold starts; reserved concurrency guarantees capacity but does not pre-warm execution environments. Consider a SendMessage A P I that must respond quickly for chat users: provisioned concurrency will ensure consistent low-latency responses, while reserved concurrency alone will not remove the initial cold-start delay. Ask yourself which requests must have guaranteed latency, and weigh that against ongoing costs for provisioned capacity.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 9.9 › Cold Starts
Cold start process
Step 1
Provision environment
AWS sets up the runtime and file system for your function.
Step 2
Initialize code
Runtime loads dependencies and runs any global initialization.
Step 3
Handle request
Handler executes business logic and returns response.
Mitigation
Use provisioned concurrency for critical, latency-sensitive functions and minimize init work.
Caution
Provisioned concurrency increases cost; validate that latency benefits justify the expense.
Concrete example
A SendMessage endpoint for chat experiences might use provisioned concurrency to ensure users never see initial delays after idle periods. Measure cold start times in CloudWatch to validate the need.
Key Takeaway

Provisioned concurrency removes cold starts for warmed environments but plan for its steady cost.

screens.title: Memory Allocation and CPU Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Lambda ties C P U allocation to memory size: when you increase memory, C P U and network throughput scale proportionally. This means a higher memory setting can reduce execution time for C P U-bound tasks, sometimes lowering total cost despite the higher per-millisecond price. To find the optimal setting, run experiments at multiple memory sizes and measure execution time and cost, because the optimal point depends on your function’s C P U profile and external input and output patterns. For example, a data-transforming function that sorts large arrays will likely benefit from more memory and C P U, while a simple request validator may not. A common mistake is to pick a default memory and never re-evaluate it; workloads change, and periodic profiling is important. Also be mindful that increasing memory for short-lived functions reduces ms but raises per-ms cost; compute the overall cost-per-invocation to decide. Use CloudWatch metrics and the SAM or other profiling tools to capture duration histograms. Finally, keep package size small and prefer native extensions only when necessary. Ask yourself: is my function C P U-bound or input and output-bound? That question guides whether memory increases will save time and money.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 9.9 › Memory & CPU
Concept

Memory controls CPU allocation in Lambda. More memory usually increases CPU and network, often reducing execution time for compute-heavy functions.

Example test
Run the same invocation at 128MB, 512MB, and 1024MB and compare average duration and cost.
Misconception
More memory always reduces cost. Not always—measure cost-per-invocation before committing to higher memory for many functions.
Practical steps
  • Identify CPU-bound functions with heavy computation.
  • Run experiments across memory sizes and record duration and billed ms.
  • Compute cost-per-invocation and choose the configuration with lowest cost for acceptable latency.
Key Takeaway

Tune memory based on measurable performance data, not assumptions about needing more RAM.

screens.title: Concurrency, Throttling, and Reserved Concurrency
screens.narratorSegment: Concurrency in Lambda determines how many execution environments can run simultaneously. AWS enforces account-level concurrency and function-level limits. Reserved concurrency sets aside a guaranteed pool for a function, preventing other functions from consuming that capacity and ensuring critical functions can scale. This is useful for protecting latency-sensitive endpoints or rate-limiting a traffic spike that might otherwise overwhelm downstream services. Throttling happens when concurrency limits are exceeded and invocations are rejected or retried. To protect downstream systems like databases, use reserved concurrency to cap the maximum parallelism a function can reach. A common error is to assume reserved concurrency removes cold starts — it does not. Reserved concurrency protects capacity but the first provisioned environment will still require initialization if not warmed, unless you also use provisioned concurrency. Another design pattern is to pair A P I Gateway throttling and usage plans with reserved concurrency so you control both ingress rate and backend capacity. Example: give your registration Lambda reserved concurrency that matches your database write capacity, and apply a gateway usage plan to limit abusive clients. Regularly review concurrency metrics and CloudWatch alarms to detect throttling early.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 9.9 › Concurrency & Throttling
Key controls
Account concurrency
A shared pool across functions for the account and region.
Reserved concurrency
Sets a guaranteed maximum for a single function and protects downstream capacity.

When concurrency is exceeded, API Gateway or clients will receive throttled responses. Use alarms on Throttles and ConcurrentExecutions to detect overloads and apply mitigation.

Design practice: coordinate reserved concurrency with database capacity and API Gateway usage plans to limit inbound request rates.

Scenario
A critical registration function should not compete with background batch jobs. Give the registration Lambda reserved concurrency so user traffic always has capacity even under heavy batch load.
Key Takeaway

Use reserved concurrency to guarantee capacity and API Gateway throttles to control client ingress.

screens.title: Event-Driven Integrations: DynamoDB, SQS, SNS, and Step Functions
screens.narratorSegment: Event-driven architecture is central to robust serverless microservices. Use DynamoDB for serverless data persistence; it scales automatically and works well as a backing store for Lambda handlers. SQS provides reliable queuing for asynchronous work and retries. SNS enables fan-out patterns where a single event triggers multiple subscribers like email, analytics, or notification Lambdas. For orchestrating complex workflows or the Saga pattern, Step Functions sequence functions and services with explicit state and retries. A practical registration flow shows this in action: the RegisterUserLambda writes user data to DynamoDB and publishes a 'User Registered' message to SNS. Subscriber Lambdas like SendWelcomeEmailLambda and UpdateAnalyticsLambda process the event asynchronously, which avoids blocking the registration request. A common mistake is making everything synchronous; blocking the initial A P I call with downstream work increases latency and coupling. Instead, return success to the caller and let asynchronous functions handle non-critical work. For workflows requiring ordered steps or compensating transactions, use Step Functions to coordinate retries and rollbacks. Design your error and retry policy carefully: SQS dead-letter queues and Step Functions error handling are essential for observability and recovery.

Module 10 › Chapter 9.9 › Event Integrations
Integration cards
DynamoDB
Serverless, fast key-value store for persistent state used by Lambda functions.
SQS
Buffered, reliable queue for asynchronous processing and retries.
SNS
Publish-subscribe fan-out for notifying multiple subscribers concurrently.
Step Functions
Coordinate multi-step workflows with state, retries, and compensation logic.
Concrete scenario
User registration: API Gateway → RegisterUserLambda → DynamoDB write → SNS publish → SendWelcomeEmail and UpdateAnalytics Lambdas subscribe. This ensures the registration API returns quickly and downstream work runs asynchronously.
Key Takeaway

Favor asynchronous, event-driven patterns to decouple services and improve responsiveness.

screens.title: SAM Template & Hello World Deployment
screens.narratorSegment: The AWS Serverless Application Model simplifies deploying Lambda and A P I Gateway resources. A simple SAM template defines the function, its runtime, memory and policies, and an A P I event that exposes an HTTP path. In the starter workflow: run sam init to scaffold a project, review template. yaml, run sam build, and then sam deploy --guided to provision the stack. After deployment, curl the published endpoint to verify the function responds. This is a quick way to validate your pipeline and IAM roles. The practice code includes a minimal function that returns a plain text greeting. Remember to check CloudWatch logs for invocation details and to confirm that the Lambda role has AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole so logs are available. A common mistake is granting overly broad IAM rights during deploy; accept the IAM creation prompts but inspect the generated role and refine policies before production. Use samconfig. toml to save deployment choices. After you validate the Hello World A P I, iterate: add input validation, connect DynamoDB, and test cold start behavior by invoking after idle periods. This hands-on validation will surface performance, permission, and integration issues in a controlled environment.

Remember to check CloudWatch logs for invocation details and to confirm that the Lambda role has AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole so logs are available. A common mistake is granting overly broad IAM rights during deploy; accept the IAM creation prompts but inspect the generated role and refine policies before production. Use samconfig. toml to save deployment choices. After you validate the Hello World A P I, iterate: add input validation, connect DynamoDB, and test cold start behavior by invoking after idle periods. screens.title: Securing Serverless APIs
screens.narratorSegment: Securing serverless APIs requires combining A P I Gateway features with least-privilege IAM for Lambda roles. A P I Gateway authorizers let you validate and authorize incoming requests before they reach your backend. Lambda authorizers provide custom authentication and authorization logic, which is useful when you have nonstandard tokens or custom identity providers. IAM authorizers leverage signed AWS requests and roles; they are suitable when callers use AWS credentials. Amazon Cognito User Pools offer a managed user directory for standard authentication flows. For Lambda functions themselves, assign IAM roles that grant only the permissions necessary for their tasks — for example, give a registration function permission to write to a specific DynamoDB table and to publish to a single SNS topic, not blanket DynamoDB or SNS access. A frequent mistake is over-permissioning roles during rapid development. Another common pitfall is placing sensitive secrets directly in environment variables; prefer AWS Secrets Manager or encrypted parameters to keep credentials safe. Also enforce TLS, use A P I Gateway usage plans to throttle abusive clients, and log authorization failures for auditing. In summary, combine the right authorizer for A P I access with minimal Lambda permissions and secure secret storage to maintain a safe serverless surface.

screens.title: Cost Optimization for Serverless Microservices
screens.narratorSegment: Serverless cost optimization focuses on matching configuration to workload so you pay only for useful work. Start by right-sizing Lambda memory: measure duration across memory settings and select the lowest cost-per-invocation for acceptable latency. Use event-driven patterns to avoid idle compute: asynchronous processing with SNS and SQS prevents long-running or idle functions. A P I Gateway offers throttling and usage plans to prevent runaway costs from unexpected request spikes. Provisioned concurrency reduces latency but increases cost because you pay for pre-initialized environments; use it only where latency guarantees are required. Take advantage of free-tier allowances when experimenting, but validate production usage with real traffic patterns. Monitor CloudWatch metrics for duration, concurrent executions, and throttles. A mistake many teams make is configuring many functions with high memory by default; this multiplies cost without always improving user experience. Also consider batching operations and using SQS to smooth traffic. Finally, instrument your functions to report duration and cost metrics so you can attribute spending and find optimization candidates. Ask: which functions consume the most compute time and would benefit most from tuning or architectural changes?

Module 10 › Chapter 9.9 › Cost Optimization
Optimization checklist
  • Measure duration and compute cost per invocation at multiple memory sizes.
  • Use event-driven processing to avoid blocking user requests.
  • Apply API Gateway throttling and usage plans to protect against traffic spikes.
  • Use provisioned concurrency only for functions with strict latency SLAs.
Practical tips
Batch work to reduce per-message overhead.
Use SQS to smooth spikes and lower peak concurrency costs.
Instrument functions to map cost to features and identify expensive handlers.
Key Takeaway

Measure, experiment, and choose the configuration that balances latency and total cost for your workload.

screens.title: Common Mistakes & Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Many serverless projects stumble on a handful of recurring issues. First, tight coupling between Lambda functions leads to brittle deployments and makes independent scaling difficult. Prefer event-driven communication and well-defined contracts. Second, missing IAM least-privilege leads to overbroad roles that increase blast radius; always scope policies to specific resources and actions. Third, ignoring cold starts for latency-sensitive APIs results in poor user experience; measure and consider provisioned concurrency for critical paths. Fourth, insufficient monitoring and logging makes troubleshooting slow; enable structured logs, duration metrics, and alarms for throttles and errors. Fifth, placing synchronous long-running tasks in the request path increases latency and risk; move non-critical work to asynchronous flows using SNS or SQS. For troubleshooting: reproduce the issue with realistic load, inspect CloudWatch logs and X-Ray traces, check concurrent execution limits, and examine invocation metrics for spikes. If you see throttles, check reserved concurrency settings and A P I Gateway usage plans. Finally, validate VPC configurations because ENI creation can add latency. These practices reduce surprises and help you diagnose issues more quickly when they occur. Common Mistakes & Troubleshooting means avoid tight coupling, overbroad iam, and synchronous long-running tasks; monitor and instrument for faster diagnosis.. In practical terms, what to watch for when building serverless microservices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Serverless microservices pair AWS Lambda with Amazon A P I Gateway to let you concentrate on business logic instead of servers. In this lesson you will learn the core roles each service plays, common integration patterns, and the operational levers you can use to tune performance and cost. We will walk through a concrete user-registration flow to illustrate asynchronous events, security via authorizers, and how to limit latency with provisioned concurrency. You will also see how integrations with DynamoDB, SQS and SNS enable resilient, decoupled microservices that scale automatically. A practical SAM deployment snippet and a short hands-on activity will show how to bootstrap a 'Hello World' A P I and validate it with curl. Finally, you will learn common mistakes to avoid — such as tight coupling between functions or underestimating cold start impact — and the safety principle of least privilege for IAM roles. By the end of this module you will be able to design a serverless microservice, choose the right A P I Gateway type, tune Lambda performance, secure endpoints, and reason about cost trade-offs. Consider how these ideas map to a user-facing A P I you manage and which knobs you would change first for latency or cost.

Over the next screens we will achieve five practical objectives that equip you to design, optimize, secure, and operate serverless microservices. First, you will learn to design and implement serverless microservices using Lambda and A P I Gateway, with clear patterns for synchronous APIs and asynchronous event wiring. Second, you will optimize Lambda performance by understanding cold starts, tuning memory and C P U trade-offs, and managing concurrency so functions remain responsive. Third, you will secure serverless APIs using A P I Gateway authorizers — exploring Lambda authorizers, IAM authorizers, and Cognito user pools — and apply the principle of least privilege to execution roles. Fourth, you will integrate serverless microservices with other AWS services such as DynamoDB, SQS, SNS, and Step Functions to build durable, decoupled workflows. Finally, you will learn how to analyze cost drivers in serverless designs, right-size resources, and use features like provisioned concurrency judiciously. Each objective pairs a concept with a small practice or mental model so you can both reason about designs and apply them in real deployments. As you proceed, notice trade-offs between latency, cost, and operational complexity, and keep an eye on common mistakes such as tight coupling and missing IAM restrictions.

This continuation of the objectives clarifies measurable outcomes and practice cues you can apply immediately. You will be able to choose between A P I Gateway types — REST, HTTP, and WebSocket — depending on latency, cost, and feature requirements. You will practice configuring authorizers and IAM policies that follow least privilege so your functions only have the permissions they need. You will gain techniques for integrating Lambda with DynamoDB, SQS, and SNS to build event-driven flows that avoid blocking user-facing requests. Finally, you will develop a cost optimization checklist: right-size memory, measure execution time, apply throttling and usage plans, and apply provisioned concurrency only when latency guarantees justify the extra cost. Each objective includes a short validation step, such as invoking the A P I after a cold start, comparing timings, and inspecting CloudWatch logs. This helps you not just understand theory but verify behavior. Keep a mental model of trade-offs: lower latency often increases cost; tighter security sometimes increases complexity. These objectives prepare you to design production-ready serverless microservices and to communicate trade-offs to stakeholders.

AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service that runs code in response to events. At its core, Lambda is event-driven and stateless: functions are invoked when triggers occur, execute business logic, and then return results or emit events. This stateless model is a strength for microservices because each function can be independently deployed and scaled without managing servers. A concrete example is a registration handler that validates input, writes to DynamoDB, and publishes an SNS event. In practice, treat Lambda as ephemeral compute: any persistent state must live in external services such as DynamoDB or S3. A common misconception is to assume in-memory state persists across invocations; while container reuse may appear to hold data, it is not guaranteed and should not be relied upon. Another important feature is pay-per-execution billing billed in 1 millisecond increments, which encourages small, focused functions. For performance, remember that memory allocation controls C P U allocation proportionally, so increasing memory can reduce execution time. Finally, when designing microservices, prefer clear single-responsibility functions and avoid tight coupling; where coordination is needed, use event mechanisms like SNS or Step Functions. Reflect on a service you maintain: what state must be externalized, and which events would you publish for decoupled processing?

Amazon A P I Gateway is the managed front door for your serverless APIs. It comes in three main flavors: REST APIs, HTTP APIs, and WebSocket APIs. REST APIs provide the fullest feature set including stages, models, and integrations; they are useful when you need advanced A P I management features. HTTP APIs are a newer alternative offering lower latency and lower cost for common RESTful patterns; they are a good fit when you want simple routing and performance. WebSocket APIs enable bidirectional, low-latency communication for real-time applications. Choosing the right type matters: for a low-latency microservice that only needs simple request/response behavior, HTTP APIs often reduce cost and improve performance. For complex versioning, request/response transformations, or advanced monitoring you might prefer REST APIs. Authorizers are another dimension: A P I Gateway supports Lambda authorizers for custom logic, IAM authorizers to use AWS credentials, and Amazon Cognito User Pools for managed user directories. A common mistake is defaulting to the full REST A P I without checking if an HTTP A P I covers your requirements — this can increase cost and latency unnecessarily. Consider the chat, IoT, or simple CRUD A P I you maintain. Which Gateway type best balances your need for features versus latency and cost?

A cold start occurs when Lambda must initialize a new execution environment before running your code. This includes setting up the runtime, pulling the code, and running any initialization logic. Cold starts are more visible for languages with heavier runtimes or large deployment packages, and for functions placed in a VPC where ENI provisioning can add latency. To mitigate cold starts, the primary tool is provisioned concurrency, which pre-initializes a defined number of execution environments so those invocations avoid cold initialization. Provisioned concurrency is ideal for latency-sensitive functions, but it increases cost because you pay for the pre-initialized environments whether they are used or not. Additional techniques include minimizing deployment package size, lazy-loading heavy dependencies, and reducing initialization work in the handler. Another approach is to use warmers or scheduled invocations to keep environments alive, but these are less reliable than provisioned concurrency and can add cost. A common misconception is to believe reserved concurrency eliminates cold starts; reserved concurrency guarantees capacity but does not pre-warm execution environments. Ask yourself which requests must have guaranteed latency, and weigh that against ongoing costs for provisioned capacity.

AWS Lambda ties C P U allocation to memory size: when you increase memory, C P U and network throughput scale proportionally. This means a higher memory setting can reduce execution time for C P U-bound tasks, sometimes lowering total cost despite the higher per-millisecond price. To find the optimal setting, run experiments at multiple memory sizes and measure execution time and cost, because the optimal point depends on your function’s C P U profile and external input and output patterns. For example, a data-transforming function that sorts large arrays will likely benefit from more memory and C P U, while a simple request validator may not. A common mistake is to pick a default memory and never re-evaluate it; workloads change, and periodic profiling is important. Also be mindful that increasing memory for short-lived functions reduces ms but raises per-ms cost; compute the overall cost-per-invocation to decide. Use CloudWatch metrics and the SAM or other profiling tools to capture duration histograms. Finally, keep package size small and prefer native extensions only when necessary. Ask yourself: is my function C P U-bound or input and output-bound? That question guides whether memory increases will save time and money.

Reserved concurrency sets aside a guaranteed pool for a function, preventing other functions from consuming that capacity and ensuring critical functions can scale. This is useful for protecting latency-sensitive endpoints or rate-limiting a traffic spike that might otherwise overwhelm downstream services. Throttling happens when concurrency limits are exceeded and invocations are rejected or retried. To protect downstream systems like databases, use reserved concurrency to cap the maximum parallelism a function can reach.
